Microsoft reported results for its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the period ended Sept. 30, 2026) on Oct. 28.
It skipped a figure it had included in each of its three prior reports: the count of paid seats for Microsoft 365 Copilot, its artificial intelligence (AI) assistant for office work.
The latest count, from July, was over 30 million.
Missed AI's "Act 1"?
Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase.
"Act 2" is the global rollout.
Continue »  The stock trades around $521 as of this writing, about 6% below the record $555.80 it closed at on Nov. 4.
From seat counts to usage stats  Microsoft began 2026 by putting a number on Copilot.
On its January earnings call, Nadella said the company had 15 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats.
By the April call, the total topped 20 million.
And by the July call, it crossed 30 million, with net seat additions more than doubling from the last quarter.
Nadella said daily Copilot users climbed almost 50% from the last quarter and more than fivefold year over year.

Customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats increased more than eightfold year over year, he added, and the count of customers using Copilot credits with usage-based billing grew more than 75% in the quarter.
She did say Copilot revenue growth picked up from the previous quarter, with continued adoption in Microsoft 365, GitHub, and security.
Story Continues    At last year's event in November 2025, Microsoft's Copilot news was mainly about products.
It introduced Agent 365, a tool for managing and securing a company's AI agents.
And it announced Microsoft 365 Copilot Business for companies with under 300 users, at $21 per user per month starting December.
On adoption, Microsoft said over 90% of the Fortune 500 use Microsoft 365 Copilot -- a usage number, not a paid one.
Copilot is still small next to Microsoft  Microsoft lists the Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on for big businesses at $30 per user per month.
Even if all 30 million seats paid that full price (unlikely, given discounts and bundles), Copilot would bring in about $11 billion a year.
Still, Microsoft posted about $347 billion in revenue over the last four quarters, so even that generous estimate is roughly 3% of the total.
By comparison, the Microsoft Cloud business alone took in $63.9 billion in the fiscal first quarter, up 30% year over year.
Microsoft's non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share were $18.04 for the four quarters through September.
At about $521, the stock trades at roughly 29 times adjusted earnings, down from about 31 times adjusted earnings at the Nov. 4 record.
A paid seat count far above 30 million, or even better a revenue number for Copilot, would show the assistant becoming a business big enough to move results at a company this size.
But I'd want to see what Copilot brings in before paying around 29 times adjusted earnings for new shares.

A value ETF for the modern market  The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF (NASDAQ:VONV) is a modern take on value stocks.

While the Vanguard Growth ETF, Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF, and Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF label most major tech-focused companies as growth stocks, the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF takes a nuanced approach.
The Russell 1000 is the 1,000 largest U.S. listed companies by market cap.
It includes smaller large-cap and mid-cap stocks, whereas the S&P 500 just has large-cap stocks.

FTSE Russell, a subsidiary of the London Stock Exchange Group, has a semi-annual reconstitution whereby it roughly splits the market cap weighting of the Russell 1000 into two indexes -- the Russell 1000 Value Index (which the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF tracks) and the Russell 1000 Growth Index -- which is mirrored by the Vanguard Russell 1000 Growth ETF.
As a result, the Russell 1000 Value ETF's three largest holdings are Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft -- which make up a combined 17.4% of the ETF as of Sept. 30.
But since all of Amazon's market cap is weighted exclusively by the value index while Apple and Microsoft are split, Amazon is actually the largest individual holding in the Russell 1000 Value ETF.

The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF has a 21.6 price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio and 1.5% dividend yield, making it less expensive and more income-focused than the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF -- which has a 24 P/E and 1.1% yield.
The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF has a dirt cheap fee structure -- charging a mere 0.06% expense ratio, or $6 for every $10,000 invested.

The ETF has crushed the S&P 500 year to date, driven by strong performance in key value-focused sectors such as energy, consumer staples, and healthcare, and the ETF's lower exposure to the semiconductor industry relative to the S&P 500.

The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF is a top buy now  The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF is a great buy for investors who view Amazon as an established cloud computing and retail giant, Apple as a modern-day consumer staple, and Microsoft as a balanced technology conglomerate with a clear runway for moderate earnings appreciation and a growing dividend.
Even with these names, the ETF is more value-focused than the S&P 500.

The ETF's 19.5% weighting in the technology sector makes it a nice middle ground between a more growth-focused index like the S&P 500 and traditional value ETFs that will exclude giant tech stocks like Apple and Microsoft.

All told, the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF is the ideal fit for investors who want to buy an ETF with leading growth stocks but who are also satisfied with their existing Nvidia holdings or want to avoid the stock altogether.

That's the view of three former Fortune 500 CEOs, and a leading consultant, whom Fortune interviewed on arguably the most consequential leadership earthquake ever to rock the business world.
On November 12, the Nvidia board issued a press release announcing Jensen Huang's resignation shortly after reports of the CEO's second affair emerged.
Kress has spent a quarter century in Big Tech financial roles, including thirteen years at Microsoft, before joining Nvidia in 2013.
(They're identified here as ex-CEOs 1, 2, and 3.)
says ex-CEO 3.

It astounds these sources that the world's second-most-valuable company, in business 33 years and public for 27, didn't have a seasoned leader long groomed for the role ready to step in—especially given that Huang will turn 64 in February, and is already the oldest CEO by far in the Mag Seven.

First: The success problem  Huang's feat of hiking Nvidia's valuation by well over $5 trillion in just four years to a peak of $5.8 trillion in early October—the highest summit ever reached—has never been equaled.
Story Continues       "No one peeled back the layers on how Nvidia was run because they were so successful," says ex-CEO 1.

In terms of percentages, its ownership resembles the profile at many Fortune 500 members: Nvidia's largest shareholders are the big institutions; Blackstone leads at 8.1%, followed by Vanguard (6.5%), State Street (4.2%), Fidelity (3.9%), and a combination of Morgan Stanley, T. Rowe Price and J.P. Morgan at around 5%.
Huang holds "just" 3.5%.
"In any company that runs well over time," says ex-CEO 2, "you'll find the board has lots of current or retired CEOs, and credible outside senior executives.
Of the seven directors excluding Huang, none has served as CEO of a Fortune 500 company, and four are mainstays of between 13 and 29 years.
"The board wasn't paying attention to how the company was run," says ex-CEO 2.
Ex-CEO 2 avows that indeed, the board's first responsibility is preparing a successor: "It's the most important thing the board does by a mile.
Ex-CEO 1 states that in the first year or two of a relatively young CEO's reign, the board may not yet have anointed their permanent replacement.
Echoing ex-CEO 1, ex-CEO 3 intones that "Boards have all kinds of governance rules but just two major responsibilities.
Third: The "too many reports" pitfall  Huang talked proudly about overseeing around 60 "direct reports," extolling the supposed virtues of a "flat" organization.
"It's highly possible that none of those lieutenants had enough responsibility to have actually been tested," notes ex-CEO 3.
Adds ex-CEO 1, "In big companies, the optimal number of direct reports is 8 to 12.
The presence of 60 direct reports that Huang was making a big deal about tells you the board wasn't doing its job."
Ex-CEO 3 believes they'd go not for a veteran in, say, their early 60s, but a young tiger in their 40s or early 50s.
"They'd want someone who is, say, 50 and wants to show the world something," says this observer.
Ex-CEO 2 concludes that the board was so excessively lax that, "If Nvidia hadn't been performing well, it would have been exhibit A for an activist attack."

The fall of Jensen Huang unleashed another kind of broadside that exposed a big need for reform, and hopefully, it will have the same legacy as a raid from outsiders: A new era where this exceptional performer masters what it's sorely lacking, and what most of the Fortune 500 already does far better: strong corporate governance.
